extracted.intended_audience: graduate students/readers learning algebraic geometry (users of Vakil's The Rising Sea)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of definitions and verifiable criteria for basic algebraic-geometric objects: discrete valuation rings, regular local rings, smooth/étale morphisms, valuative criteria for separatedness/properness, and the Artin–Rees lemma. Targets readers who need the precise local/presentation conditions and logical equivalences used to check these properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: Noetherian local domain dim 1 ⇔ DVR
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.5.6: An integral domain A is a Noetherian local ring of dimension 1 satisfying (a)–(d) if and only if (e) A is a discrete valuation ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an equivalence: checking the listed Noetherian/local/dimension/regular-type hypotheses (a)–(d) is equivalent to A being a discrete valuation ring. (See surrounding exercises that show v is a discrete valuation and converses.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of discrete valuation on a DVR
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 13.5.F: Show that there is only one discrete valuation on a discrete valuation ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intended check: if A is a DVR then the associated valuation on its fraction field is unique (i.e., the valuation giving the valuation ring A is uniquely determined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of zero/pole via valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 13.5.7: If the valuation v(f) = n > 0, f has a zero of order n; if v(f) = -n < 0, f has a pole of order n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the operational notion of order of vanishing/pole at a regular codimension 1 point (where O_{X,p} is a DVR). It is the basis for counting zeros/poles on schemes and for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: regular local ring dim 1 ⇔ unique factorization domain ⇔ integrally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.5.8: For a Noetherian local ring of dimension 1, the conditions (a)–(e) (including being a DVR) are equivalent to (f) A is a unique factorization domain and (g) A is integrally closed in its fraction field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch given: (a)–(e) ⇒ (f) by explicit factorization u t^n; (f) ⇒ (g) since UFDs are integrally closed; and (g) ⇒ (a)–(e) via arguments that m becomes principal, etc. Use these equivalences to check/replace properties in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeros and poles of rational functions are finite on integral Noetherian schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 13.5.G: If X is an integral Noetherian scheme and f is a nonzero element of K(X)×, then f has a finite number of zeros and poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to Spec A and writing f = f1/f2 with fi ∈ A; use Noetherian properties to show finiteness. This is the algebraic analogue of 'a rational function has finitely many zeros/poles.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic Hartogs: regularity from absence of poles
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 13.5.H: If f is a nonzero rational function on a locally Noetherian normal scheme and f has no poles, then f is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint references Algebraic Hartogs’s Lemma 12.3.14; used to deduce extendability of functions when no poles are present on normal Noetherian schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedekind domain definition and localization property
rubrics_metrics.description: §13.5.16: A Dedekind domain is a Noetherian integral domain of dimension at most one that is normal (integrally closed). The localization at any nonzero prime (codimension one) is a discrete valuation ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: rings of integers in number fields are examples; nonzero ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals. Use localization at height-1 primes to pass to DVRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of smooth morphism (local presentation + Jacobian condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 13.6.2: A morphism π: X → Y is smooth of relative dimension n if there exist open covers {Ui} of X and {Vi} of Y with π(Ui) ⊂ Vi and for each i a commutative diagram identifying Ui with an open W ⊂ Spec B[x1,...,xn+r]/(f1,...,fr) where det(∂fj/∂xi)_{1≤i,j≤r} is invertible on W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central verifiable criterion: locally on the source, X is an open in the vanishing locus of r equations in n+r variables and the r×r minor of the Jacobian matrix has invertible determinant (Jacobian condition). Étale = smooth of relative dimension 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of smoothness: locally of finite presentation and openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick observations (13.6.3): From the definition, smooth morphisms are locally of finite presentation (hence locally of finite type); the locus on X where π is smooth of relative dimension n is open; the étale locus is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking smoothness, one can assert finiteness-type properties and that smoothness is an open condition; use this to reduce checks to local neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic examples and permanence properties of smooth/étale morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations and exercises (13.6.3–13.6.D): Open embeddings are étale; projection A^n_Y → Y is smooth of relative dimension n; smoothness is local on source and target, preserved by base change, stable under composition, and closed under products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving a morphism is smooth/étale, check local charts or factor it into known smooth/étale maps (e.g., étale followed by projection). Use base-change and composition to build new examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local factorization near a point: étale + projection
rubrics_metrics.description: 13.6.4 Observation: If π: X → Y is smooth of relative dimension n, then locally on X the map can be factored as U --α→ A^n_Y --β→ Y where α is étale and β is projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the local shape of a smooth map: an étale map into affine space followed by projection. Useful to reduce local questions about smooth maps to étale/local-isomorphism type questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of definitions of smoothness over a field
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.6.5: For a k-scheme X, X is smooth of relative dimension n over Spec k (Def.13.6.2) iff X has pure dimension n and is smooth over k in the sense of the earlier Jacobian/tangent-space condition (Def.13.2.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This confirms compatibility of the general (scheme) definition with the classical differential/Jacobian criteria over fields. Use closed-point/local tangent space checks to verify smoothness over fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuative criterion for separatedness (DVR version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.7.1 (DVR version): For π: X → Y of finite type between locally Noetherian schemes, π is separated iff for every discrete valuation ring A and every commutative diagram Spec K(A) → X over Spec A → Y, there is at most one morphism Spec A → X making the diagram commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational test: to check separatedness in this setting, verify uniqueness of extensions from maps defined on the generic point (Spec K(A)) to maps defined on the whole DVR. The book gives geometric intuition (germ of a curve) and exercises for the easy direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuative criterion for separatedness (general valuation rings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.7.4: For a quasiseparated morphism π: X → Y, π is separated iff for any valuation ring A with function field K and any diagram Spec K → X over Spec A → Y, there is at most one morphism Spec A → X commuting with the diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the DVR-version to arbitrary valuation rings; proofs referenced to Stacks/ÉGA. Use when DVR hypotheses are too restrictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuative criterion for universal closedness and properness (DVR version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.7.6: For π: X → Y of finite type between locally Noetherian schemes, π is universally closed (resp. proper) iff for any DVR A and any diagram Spec K(A) → X over Spec A → Y, there is at least one (resp. exactly one) morphism Spec A → X making the diagram commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: properness = existence and uniqueness of limits for one-parameter families (maps from punctured DVRs). Use this to test properness/universal-closedness in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuative criterion for universal closedness/properness (general valuation rings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.7.9: For quasiseparated, finite type π: X → Y, π is universally closed (resp. proper) iff for any valuation ring A and diagram Spec K → X over Spec A → Y, there is at least one (resp. exactly one) extension Spec A → X making the diagram commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full generalization of the DVR-version; proofs cited in standard references. Use for moduli/properness checks when rank>1 valuations matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moduli interpretation of valuative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks 13.7.2/13.7.7: For a (fine) moduli space X over a field k, separatedness means at most one extension of a family over a punctured DVR; properness means always exactly one extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the conceptual way to use valuative criteria when interpreting separatedness/properness in moduli problems: uniqueness/existence of extensions of families parametrized by punctured DVRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localizations of regular local rings remain regular
rubrics_metrics.description: 13.8.1 and Fact 13.8.2: If (A,m) is a regular local ring, then any localization of A at a prime is also a regular local ring (Corollary-type fact; references given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: to check regularity of a Noetherian scheme it suffices to check closed points (maximal ideals) provided the fact is available; local behavior is preserved under localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity from closed points for finite type over perfect field
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 13.8.3: If X is a finite type scheme over a perfect field k and X is regular at its closed points, then X is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful geometric criterion: for finite type schemes over perfect fields, checking regularity at closed points suffices to conclude regularity everywhere (exercise and later chapters give generalizations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings: factorial, integrally closed, Cohen-Macaulay
rubrics_metrics.description: 13.8.4–13.8.8 (Facts/Remarks): Regular local rings are unique factorization domains (Auslander–Buchsbaum theorem), hence integrally closed, and are Cohen–Macaulay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are major structural properties to be used as black-box facts (proofs are nontrivial). The text warns that factoriality is strictly weaker than regularity with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rees algebra finite-generation ⇔ I-stability of filtration
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 13.9.2: For A Noetherian and M finitely generated, a descending I-filtration M = M0 ⊃ M1 ⊃ ... is I-stable iff the associated graded/rees-type module M• = ⊕_{n≥0} Mn is a finitely generated module over A•(I) = ⊕_{n≥0} I^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an algebraic criterion to test whether a filtration stabilizes: check finite generation of the Rees algebra/module. The proof uses Noetherianness and standard graded-module arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artin–Rees lemma (stability of intersections with filtrations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artin–Rees Lemma 13.9.3: Suppose A is Noetherian, M is a finitely generated A-module with an I-stable filtration (Mn), and L ⊂ M is a submodule. Let Ln := L ∩ Mn. Then (Ln) is an I-stable filtration of L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: intersections of submodules with an I-stable filtration inherit stability. This is the key technical lemma used in many finiteness/continuity arguments (e.g., Cohomology and Base Change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artin–Rees corollary for I-adic filtration
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 13.9.4: If I is an ideal of a Noetherian ring A, M a finitely generated A-module, and L ⊂ M, then there exists s such that for all d ≥ 0, I^d (L ∩ I^s M) = L ∩ I^{d+s} M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard consequence: eventually the intersections with powers of I are controlled by a fixed shift s. Useful for Krull intersection type arguments and proving continuity results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull Intersection consequences (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 13.9.A: For I an ideal in a Noetherian ring A and M finitely generated, (a) there is an a such that ⋂_{j=1}^∞ I^j M = 0 under suitable hypotheses; (b) if A is Noetherian domain or Noetherian local and I proper then ⋂ I^j = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Artin–Rees and Nakayama lemma. This provides a practical criterion: in many Noetherian/local/domain contexts the intersection of all powers of a proper ideal is zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: intersection formulas may fail without shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning (13.9.4 discussion): It need not be true that I^d L = L ∩ I^d M for all d; a counterexample may be constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care when reasoning about intersections vs. ideal multiplications; apply Artin–Rees to obtain correct shifted equalities rather than naive equalities.
